questions.stem: A practical case: Sana Garcia deposits $4,500 in an account paying 6% simple interest for 5 years. How much interest is earned over the full term?

options.misconception: counts only one year of interest instead of the whole term

questions.stem: Work through this: Bilal Mensah invests $1,000 at 5% interest compounded annually for 2 years. What is the balance at the end?

options.misconception: uses one fewer compounding period than stated
uses simple interest instead of annual compounding
reports interest earned rather than the ending balance

questions.explanation: Compounding applies the growth rate to the previous balance each year, so the balance is principal times one plus the rate raised to the number of years. That gives $1,102.5 after 2 years. Simple interest, interest alone, or the wrong period count each misses part of the effect.
questions.hint: Compound growth uses an exponent equal to the number of years.

questions.learningObjective: Apply compound growth and time value concepts to realistic financial decisions
questions.stem: Work through this: Lucia Wong deposits $2,300 in an account paying 2% simple interest for 5 years. How much interest is earned over the full term?

options.misconception: adds the principal, giving the balance rather than the interest

questions.hint: Use I = P times r times t, with r as a decimal.

questions.stem: A practical case: At an annual return of 8%, about how many years will it take an investment to double in value?

questions.subject: PERSONAL_FINANCE
questions.learningObjective: Apply compound growth and time value concepts to realistic financial decisions
questions.stem: Here is the case: Caleb Osei wants $10,000 in 2 years. At an annual return of 6%, how much must be invested today to reach that goal?

options.misconception: compounds the goal forward instead of discounting it back
ignores the number of years entirely
uses simple discounting rather than annual discounting

questions.explanation: A future goal is discounted back to today by dividing by one plus the rate for each year, which gives $8,899.96. Compounding the goal forward or ignoring the time period produces a number that is not the amount needed now.
questions.hint: Discount the future goal back to the present.

questions.subject: PERSONAL_FINANCE
questions.learningObjective: Apply compound growth and time value concepts to realistic financial decisions
questions.stem: Here is the case: An investment earns 5% over a year while inflation runs at 4%. Approximately what is the real return?

options.misconception: multiplies the two rates together
ignores inflation entirely
adds inflation instead of subtracting it

questions.explanation: The approximate real return is the nominal return minus inflation, which is 1% here. Inflation erodes purchasing power, so adding it or ignoring it does not describe what the investor actually gained.
questions.hint: Subtract the inflation rate from the nominal return.

questions.learningObjective: Apply compound growth and time value concepts to realistic financial decisions
questions.stem: Here is the case: Jasmine Reyes deposits $2,200 in an account paying 8% simple interest for 5 years. How much interest is earned over the full term?

options.misconception: counts only one year of interest instead of the whole term
adds the principal, giving the balance rather than the interest

questions.explanation: Simple interest equals principal times rate times time, with the rate written as a decimal. Here that is $2,200 times 8% times 5 years, which gives $880. One year of interest or the ending balance would answer a different question.
questions.hint: Use I = P times r times t, with r as a decimal.

questions.subject: PERSONAL_FINANCE
questions.learningObjective: Apply compound growth and time value concepts to realistic financial decisions
questions.stem: Work through this: At an annual return of 3%, about how many years will it take an investment to double in value?

options.misconception: subtracts the rate from seventy-two instead of dividing
multiplies by the rate instead of dividing
uses one hundred instead of the rule's seventy-two

questions.explanation: The rule of seventy-two approximates doubling time as seventy-two divided by the annual rate expressed as a percent. With a 3% return that is about 24 years. Multiplying the numbers or using a different numerator does not give a doubling time.
questions.hint: Divide seventy-two by the percentage rate.

questions.learningObjective: Apply compound growth and time value concepts to realistic financial decisions
questions.stem: Here is the case: Leila Kaur invests $4,500 at 5% interest compounded annually for 3 years. What is the balance at the end?

options.misconception: reports interest earned rather than the ending balance
uses simple interest instead of annual compounding
uses one fewer compounding period than stated

questions.explanation: Compounding applies the growth rate to the previous balance each year, so the balance is principal times one plus the rate raised to the number of years. That gives $5,209.31 after 3 years. Simple interest, interest alone, or the wrong period count each misses part of the effect.
questions.hint: Compound growth uses an exponent equal to the number of years.
